claims.text: The initial NbMoTaW alloy is equal-atomic.
The initial NbMoTaW alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical strength and heat-softening resistance at approximately 1600 °C.
NbMoTaW has poor room-temperature ductility.
The irradiation resistance of NbMoTaW has only been inferred computationally and is not experimentally verified.
Adding approximately 5 at% V and applying an optimized heat treatment will generate V-rich precipitates in NbMoTaW.
The V-rich precipitates will be nanoscale, coherent, and uniformly distributed.
Heat treatment near 1200 °C for several hours can be adjusted to control V-rich precipitate nucleation, size, and distribution.
Vacuum arc melting is an applicable synthesis route for the refractory NbMoTaW-based alloy.
V-rich precipitates will lower the critical stress for dislocation nucleation.
Lowering the critical stress for dislocation nucleation will improve room-temperature ductility.
V-rich precipitates will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects, including helium bubbles.
Defect-sink behavior will mitigate helium blistering and irradiation-enhanced precipitation.
The V addition and resulting precipitates will not significantly alter the BCC phase needed for high-temperature strength.
The V-modified alloy will have greater room-temperature plastic strain than untreated NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will accumulate fewer irradiation defects, helium bubbles, or blisters than untreated NbMoTaW.
The V-modified alloy will preserve high-temperature mechanical performance up to approximately 1600 °C.
The irradiation-tolerance improvement will apply at helium implantation energies typical of fusion environments.
Maintaining precipitate coherence and limiting coarsening are necessary to avoid loss of elevated-temperature strength.
The engineered V-rich precipitates will remain stable under room-temperature loading and elevated-temperature conditions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis promises maintenance or XRD verification of a single-phase BCC structure while also requiring a dispersion of V-rich precipitates. Unless these are explicitly defined as coherent compositional fluctuations within the same BCC phase, precipitate formation implies an additional phase and conflicts with the single-phase claim and the rule treating secondary-phase formation as falsifying.
